positions/dionysian-angelic-hierarchy/on: God created a vast, ordered world of pure spirits arranged in nine orders and three triads, through which divine light, purification and knowledge are mediated down the chain of being.
positions/dionysian-angelic-hierarchy/co: Angels are created, incorporeal intelligences serving God’s glory and human salvation.
They are ordered in three triads of three: seraphim, cherubim, thrones; dominions, powers, authorities; principalities, archangels, angels.
Hierarchy is participation in God’s light, not domination.
The heavenly liturgy is mirrored in the Church’s liturgy and clergy.
positions/dionysian-angelic-hierarchy/or: Compiled from biblical names by Pseudo-Dionysius (c.500) and, with a different order, Gregory the Great (Homily 34, c.591); systematised by Aquinas and Bonaventure; celebrated in Orthodox liturgy (Synaxis of the Archangels, 8 November).
positions/dionysian-angelic-hierarchy/st: It gathers scattered biblical names into a coherent vision of an ordered creation.
It has shaped liturgy, art and devotion East and West for 1,500 years.
It expresses a cosmos alive with worship, in which humans join the angels’ praise.
Protestant Reformers (Calvin, Luther) dismissed detailed hierarchies as idle speculation beyond Scripture.
Scholars showed the author was not Paul’s convert (Valla, Erasmus), undermining its quasi-apostolic authority.
Critics argue its Neoplatonic chain of being distances God and legitimises earthly hierarchies.
positions/dionysian-angelic-hierarchy/re: Defenders reply that the hierarchy is an aid to contemplation, held with appropriate reserve, and that its theology of participation keeps God immediately present.
Orthodox and Catholics note that authority derives from the Church’s reception, not the pseudonym.
positions/dionysian-angelic-hierarchy/co: Shaped Gothic architecture (Suger), medieval cosmology, Dante and iconography.
Remains part of Orthodox and Catholic devotion.
positions/guardian-angels/oneLine: God assigns angels to watch over individuals, communities and nations, protecting them, prompting them toward good and presenting their prayers to God.
positions/guardian-angels/coreClaims/0: Every person (or at least every believer) has a guardian angel.
positions/guardian-angels/coreClaims/1: Angels also guard churches and nations (Daniel 10-12; Revelation 2-3).
positions/guardian-angels/coreClaims/2: Angels serve God’s providence but are not to be worshipped.
positions/guardian-angels/coreClaims/3: Devotion to one’s guardian angel is commended (Catholic, Orthodox).
positions/guardian-angels/origin: Found in Second Temple Judaism and early Christian texts (Shepherd of Hermas, Origen, Basil, Jerome); taught by Aquinas (ST I q.113); feast instituted locally and made universal by Clement X (1670); common in Orthodox prayer.
positions/guardian-angels/proponentsOthe: Orthodox canon to the guardian angel
positions/guardian-angels/strongestArgum: Jesus says the little ones’ angels always behold the Father’s face (Matthew 18:10).
It expresses God’s personal providential care.
positions/guardian-angels/strongestObjec: Calvin judged it uncertain whether each believer has a particular angel, preferring to say all angels care for each.
Critics warn of devotional excess or angel-centred spirituality (as in New Age angelology).
Some scholars read Matthew 18:10 and Acts 12:15 as reflecting popular belief rather than teaching it.
positions/guardian-angels/responses/0: Defenders answer that the doctrine is held modestly and always subordinates angels to Christ.
positions/guardian-angels/responses/1: Liturgical tradition (feast of 2 October) disciplines devotion.
positions/guardian-angels/consequences/0: Shaped children’s prayers and Catholic and Orthodox piety.
positions/guardian-angels/consequences/1: Revived in popular culture, sometimes detached from Christian theology.
positions/fall-of-angels-pride/name: Satan as a fallen angel (classical doctrine)
positions/fall-of-angels-pride/oneLine: Satan and the demons were created good as angels but freely rebelled against God, chiefly through pride, before (or at) the fall of humanity; they now oppose God’s purposes but are defeated by Christ and destined for judgement.
positions/fall-of-angels-pride/coreClaim: God created all spirits good; evil is not an eternal principle (against dualism).
Some angels fell by their own free choice, led by Satan.
Their fall is irrevocable (Aquinas) or, in Origen’s speculation, possibly remediable.
Satan tempts, accuses and deceives, but is a defeated enemy (Colossians 2:15).
positions/fall-of-angels-pride/origin: Developed by Origen (c.230) and Augustine (City of God XI-XII, c.417) — who rejected the older Enochic reading of Genesis 6 — and defined against Cathar dualism by the Fourth Lateran Council (1215); the 553 anathemas rejected the restoration of demons.
positions/fall-of-angels-pride/strongest: It explains evil without dualism: evil is a corruption of good creation.
It accounts for New Testament teaching on Satan as a real personal adversary.
It provides a cosmic setting for the human fall and redemption.
Biblical scholars note that Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 refer in context to the kings of Babylon and Tyre, not Satan.
Demythologisers argue that a personal devil belongs to an obsolete world-view.
Others ask how perfectly good creatures in God’s presence could fall.
positions/fall-of-angels-pride/responses: Defenders answer that the doctrine rests chiefly on New Testament texts (John 8:44; Jude 6; Revelation 12) and that the prophetic texts were read typologically.
They argue that the mystery of the first sin, angelic or human, is inherent in genuine freedom.
positions/fall-of-angels-pride/consequen: Shaped Christian art, literature (Dante, Milton) and the theology of evil.
Underpins all later demonology and exorcism.
positions/watchers-tradition/name: The Watchers and the origin of demons (Enochic)
positions/watchers-tradition/oneLine: Rebellious angels (the Watchers) descended, took human wives and taught forbidden knowledge; their giant offspring were destroyed in the Flood and their disembodied spirits became the demons that afflict humanity.
positions/watchers-tradition/coreClaims/: “The sons of God” in Genesis 6:2 are angels.
Angelic transgression introduced violence, sorcery and idolatry into the world.
Demons are the spirits of the giants.
The fallen angels are bound in darkness until judgement (1 Enoch 10; Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4).
positions/watchers-tradition/origin: Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36, 3rd century BC); followed by Justin Martyr (2 Apology 5), Athenagoras, Irenaeus, Tertullian and others; set aside in the West after Augustine; 1 Enoch remains canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.
positions/watchers-tradition/proponentsO: Some modern evangelical scholars (e.g. Michael Heiser)
positions/watchers-tradition/strongestAr: It is the reading most Second Temple Jews and the earliest Christian writers gave to Genesis 6.
Jude quotes 1 Enoch and 2 Peter alludes to the binding of angels.
It explains the origin of demons as distinct from fallen angels.
positions/watchers-tradition/strongestOb: Augustine and later commentators argued that angels, being spirits, cannot marry (Matthew 22:30) and read “sons of God” as the line of Seth.
Most churches do not treat 1 Enoch as canonical.
Critics see it as mythological speculation.
positions/watchers-tradition/responses/0: Defenders note that Matthew 22:30 refers to angels “in heaven”, not fallen ones, and that the canonical New Testament endorses parts of the tradition.
positions/watchers-tradition/responses/1: The Ethiopian church regards its broader canon as preserving ancient apostolic usage.
positions/watchers-tradition/consequence: Shaped early Christian demonology and the Ethiopian Christian world-view.
Revived in recent evangelical biblical theology of the “divine council”.
positions/catholic-solemn-exorcism/oneLi: In cases of genuine demonic possession, discerned with medical and psychiatric help, a priest authorised by the bishop performs the Church’s rite of solemn exorcism in Christ’s name; minor exorcisms are part of baptism and ordinary prayer.
positions/catholic-solemn-exorcism/coreC: Christ gave his Church authority over demons (Mark 16:17).
Possession is rare and must be carefully distinguished from mental illness.
Only a priest with the bishop’s express permission may perform a solemn exorcism (Canon 1172).
Minor exorcisms occur in every baptism; prayers of deliverance are open to all.
positions/catholic-solemn-exorcism/origi: Exorcists were a minor order by the 3rd century (Cornelius of Rome, 251); exorcism regulated in the Rituale Romanum (1614); revised in De exorcismis (1999); promoted by figures such as Gabriele Amorth (International Association of Exorcists, 1990).
positions/catholic-solemn-exorcism/stron: It continues Jesus’ own ministry and an unbroken practice of the Church.
It is carefully regulated, requiring discernment and medical consultation.
It integrates exorcism within sacramental life rather than charismatic personality.
Psychiatrists and critics warn of misdiagnosing mental illness; deaths during exorcisms (e.g. Anneliese Michel, Germany, 1976) caused scandal.
Protestants object to ritual formulas as potentially magical.
Secular critics see it as superstition that popular media sensationalise.
positions/catholic-solemn-exorcism/respo: Catholic authorities answer that the 1999 rite was revised precisely to require medical discernment and forbids publicity.
They stress that exorcism is prayer to Christ, not a technique.
positions/catholic-solemn-exorcism/conse: Demand for exorcism has grown in Italy, Africa, Latin America and the United States since the 1990s.
positions/orthodox-exorcism-prayers/name: Orthodox and Oriental exorcism and prayers of deliverance
positions/orthodox-exorcism-prayers/altN: exorcism prayers of Basil and Chrysostom
positions/orthodox-exorcism-prayers/oneL: The Church’s whole life — baptism with its exorcisms and renunciation of Satan, holy water, the sign of the cross, fasting, the Jesus Prayer and the exorcism prayers of the service books — is spiritual warfare; priests read prayers of exorcism for the afflicted.
positions/orthodox-exorcism-prayers/core: Every baptism includes exorcisms and the renunciation of Satan facing west.
The service books contain exorcism prayers attributed to Basil and John Chrysostom.
Ascetic struggle and the Jesus Prayer guard against demonic thoughts.
In the Ethiopian and Coptic churches, holy water (tsebel) and priestly prayer are central to healing from spirit affliction.
positions/orthodox-exorcism-prayers/orig: Rooted in early baptismal practice (Apostolic Tradition, Cyril of Jerusalem), the desert fathers (Antony, Evagrius) and the Byzantine Euchologion; living practice in Greek, Russian, Coptic, Ethiopian and Syriac churches.
positions/orthodox-exorcism-prayers/stro: It integrates deliverance into the sacramental and ascetic life rather than isolating it.
It draws on an unbroken patristic tradition.
It speaks to cultures where spirit affliction is a lived reality, as in Ethiopia and Egypt.
Protestant critics question holy water and sign-of-the-cross practices as quasi-magical.
Psychiatric critics raise the same concerns as for Catholic exorcism.
Some Orthodox clergy worry about sensational “exorcist-priests” attracting crowds.
positions/orthodox-exorcism-prayers/resp: Orthodox answer that sacramentals are prayer embodied, effective only through Christ and faith.
Hierarchs regulate exorcists and emphasise confession and repentance.
positions/orthodox-exorcism-prayers/cons: Keeps a strong sense of spiritual warfare in Eastern Christian spirituality.
Ethiopian and Coptic healing sites draw Christians and non-Christians alike.
positions/pentecostal-deliverance/oneLin: Believers, empowered by the Spirit, share Jesus’ authority to cast out demons; people, including Christians, may be “demonised” (oppressed) in areas of life through sin, trauma or occult involvement and can be freed through renunciation, prayer and command in Jesus’ name.
positions/pentecostal-deliverance/coreCl: Every Spirit-filled believer has authority over demons (Mark 16:17; Luke 10:19).
Demonisation ranges from oppression to possession; Christians can be oppressed in some areas.
Doorways include sin, occult practice, trauma and generational curses.
Deliverance is part of the full gospel with healing and salvation.
positions/pentecostal-deliverance/origin: Practised from early Pentecostal revivals (Azusa Street, 1906) and healing evangelists; systematised in the charismatic movement by Derek Prince, Don Basham and Frank and Ida Mae Hammond (Pigs in the Parlor, 1973); central in Latin American (Carlos Annacondia) and African Pentecostalism.
positions/pentecostal-deliverance/propon: Mountain of Fire and Miracles Ministries (Nigeria)
positions/pentecostal-deliverance/strong: It takes seriously the large share of Jesus’ ministry spent on deliverance.
It meets real needs in cultures where spiritual oppression is widely experienced.
Many testify to lasting freedom and changed lives.
Critics (cessationist and others) argue that Christians indwelt by the Spirit cannot be demonised and that the concept fosters fear and blame-shifting.
Psychologists warn of harm when mental illness is treated as demonic.
Abuses include violent deliverances and, in some contexts, accusations of child witchcraft.
positions/pentecostal-deliverance/respon: Many practitioners now stress pastoral care, cooperation with medicine and “truth encounter” rather than “power encounter” (Neil Anderson).
They argue that abuse does not negate legitimate ministry, as with any ministry.
positions/pentecostal-deliverance/conseq: Deliverance is a major feature of global Pentecostalism, especially in Africa and Latin America.
Produced a large popular literature and prayer movements.
